ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The project was approved by the Research Ethics Review Committee of the Department of Psychology, Education and Child Studies at Erasmus University Rotterdam (application number ETH2425-0676).
A total of N = 98 participants completed the Generic Conspiracist Beliefs (GCB) scale and an animal verbal fluency task (𝑀 𝑎𝑔𝑒 = 27.88, 𝑆𝐷 𝑎𝑔𝑒 = 11.45; 59.18% female; 69.39% European).
Participants were grouped according to their levels of conspiracy thinking (high or low) and political extremity (moderate or extreme).
We recruited participants through social media platforms using a snowball sampling technique.
All participants provided informed consent.
Most participants were non-native English speakers (80.4%).
Participants completed two verbal fluency tasks adapted for online administration.
In the Animal Fluency Task, participants were given 60 seconds to type as many animal names as they can (Moreno-Martínez, 2017).
Participants gave their responses on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = definitely not true to5 = definitely true).
We conducted the study via an online Qualtrics survey (www.qualtrics.com).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .07", Sentence = "This difference was not statistically significant when 50% of the nodes were retained F(1, 1997) = 3.19, p = .07, η²p = .001."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: This study addresses a gap in previous research by examining how semantic memory organization relates to conspiracy endorsement and political extremism.
A total of N = 98 participants completed the Generic Conspiracist Beliefs (GCB) scale and an animal verbal fluency task (𝑀 𝑎𝑔𝑒 = 27.88, 𝑆𝐷 𝑎𝑔𝑒 = 11.45; 59.18% female; 69.39% European).
Of these, n = 96 also completed a self-placement political extremism item.
Participants were grouped according to their levels of conspiracy thinking (high or low) and political extremity (moderate or extreme).

We hypothesized that 1) political extremism would predict conspiracy thinking, 2) that individuals high in conspiracy thinking would exhibit flexible semantic networks, similar to those found in creative individuals, and that 3) politically extreme participants would exhibit similar semantic patterns to participants high in conspiracy thinking.

Semantic networks were constructed from verbal fluency responses, and we compared the respective group networks' clustering coefficient (CC), average shortest path length (ASPL), modularity (Q), and small-world-ness (S).
Results showed that political extremism negatively predicted conspiracy thinking.
High conspiracists exhibited more flexible semantic networks, consistent with patterns previously observed in creative individuals.
Politically extreme individuals showed efficient global connectivity but lacked local associative clustering.
These findings suggest that semantic memory structure is meaningfully linked to conspiratorial and ideological beliefs.
Longitudinal research is needed to clarify the causal direction of these associations.
Conspiracy thinking and political extremism are two phenomena that attracted considerable attention in recent research (Douglas, 2021; Swami et al., 2024; van Prooijen et al., 2015).

text.text: A total of N = 159 individuals participated in the survey.
We recruited participants through social media platforms using a snowball sampling technique.
They participated on a voluntary basis and were not compensated for their participation.
All participants provided informed consent.
The project was approved by the Research Ethics Review Committee of the Department of Psychology, Education and Child Studies at Erasmus University Rotterdam (application number ETH2425-0676).

We excluded participants who rated their writing English proficiency below CEFR level B1 (Council of Europe, 2020) to ensure reliable measurement of verbal fluency and accurate interpretation of the Generic Conspiracist Belief scale (GCBS; Brotherton et al., 2013).

text.text: We also excluded participants who did not report their age or failed to complete the GCBS.
This resulted in a sample of N = 98 participants, with a mean age of M = 27.88 years (SD = 11.45).

The sample was predominantly European (69.39%), followed by North American (10.20%), middle eastern (4.08%), Latin American (3.06%), Asian (3.06%), and participants with mixed or other national backgrounds (10.20%).
Most participants were non-native English speakers (80.4%).
The majority (77%) obtained a higher education degree (associate, bachelor's, or master's), while 21.43% reported having only a high school education.

Regarding political views, 31.63% of participants reported "slightly leaning toward one side", 32.65% described themselves as "strongly committed to one side but open to discussion", 12.24% identified as "very extreme, I believe radical change is necessary", 21.43% described themselves as "very moderate, I avoid extreme positions", and 2.04% chose "other".
Of the final sample (N = 98), we excluded participants who chose "other" on the political extremism item, resulting in n = 96 participants for the extremism analysis.

text.text: Material 2.2.1 Demographic Questionnaire.
Participants reported their age, gender, nationality, highest level of education, and criminal history.

text.text: Cleaning included standardizing responses (lowercasing, trimming whitespace), removing duplicates and spelling errors, and validating responses using predefined semantic dictionaries for animals.

text.text: Building on the semantic network framework developed by Kenett et al. (2016), we constructed semantic networks using Pearson's correlations as an association metric, which quantify the co-occurrence of word pairs across participants' verbal fluency responses.

(2016)</ref>, we constructed semantic networks using Pearson's correlations as an association metric, which quantify the co-occurrence of word pairs across participants' verbal fluency responses.

text.text: We created a binary word-by-participant matrix.
Each row corresponded to a participant and each column represented a unique word generated by the sample.
We coded the cell as 1 if the participant produced the word and 0 otherwise.
The Pearson's correlation between each pairs of word columns was calculated, resulting in a word-by-word correlation matrix.
This matrix represented how similar words were used across participants, with higher correlations indicating that two words tended to be produced by the same individuals.

The resulting correlation matrix was an unweighted, undirected semantic network, where nodes represent words and edges represent the strength of their co-occurrence across participants (Christensen & Kenett, 2023; Kenett et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The resulting correlation matrix was an unweighted, undirected semantic network, where nodes represent words and edges represent the strength of their co-occurrence across participants <ref type="bibr">(Christensen & Kenett, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kenett et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: To reduce the likelihood of including spurious associations, we employed Triangulated Maximally Filtered Graphs (TMFG) for network filtering (Massara et al., 2017).
text.formatted: To reduce the likelihood of including spurious associations, we employed Triangulated Maximally Filtered Graphs (TMFG) for network filtering <ref type="bibr">(Massara et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: TMFG preserves strong correlations and filters out weak ones.
This approach has the advantage of standardizing the ratio of edges to nodes (Christensen et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This approach has the advantage of standardizing the ratio of edges to nodes <ref type="bibr">(Christensen et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: For each group-level network, the ASPL, CC, AND Q were extracted.
We then conducted a random network analysis comparison to extract the measures needed for the S index (Christensen et al., 2018; Kenett et al., 2016).

text.text: The SemNet Shiny application is an interactive tool for semantic network analysis and is part of the SemNet package (Christensen, 2023).
text.formatted: The SemNet Shiny application is an interactive tool for semantic network analysis and is part of the SemNet package <ref type="bibr">(Christensen, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For both the group comparisons of conspiracy thinking (high vs. low) and political extremism (extreme vs. moderate), we used a node-wise bootstrapping approach.
This procedure repeatedly selects 50% of the nodes in each network without replacement and constructs partial networks for each group based on the same subset of nodes.
This process was repeated 1,000 times.

The underlying logic is that if the overall network of one group differs from that of another group, then any subnetwork from one group is likely to differ from any subnetwork of the other (Christensen & Kenett, 2023).
text.formatted: The underlying logic is that if the overall network of one group differs from that of another group, then any subnetwork from one group is likely to differ from any subnetwork of the other <ref type="bibr">(Christensen & Kenett, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For each partial network, the procedure resampled individual participants' responses within each group to compute a distribution of ASPL, CC, and Q. We then conducted an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) to examine whether partial network structures differed between groups categorized by levels of conspiracy thinking or political extremism.
Although TMFG standardizes the ratio of edges to nodes, the total number of edges in each network still depends on the number of unique responses provided (Massara et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Although TMFG standardizes the ratio of edges to nodes, the total number of edges in each network still depends on the number of unique responses provided <ref type="bibr">(Massara et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, slight differences in the number of nodes across networks can lead to differences in the overall number of edges and network density.
To account for these residual differences, we included the number of edges as a covariate in our ANCOVA analyses.
This allowed us to statistically control for network size and density when comparing network metrics between groups (Christensen & Kenett, 2023).
text.formatted: This allowed us to statistically control for network size and density when comparing network metrics between groups <ref type="bibr">(Christensen & Kenett, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, we conducted a Random Network Analysis using the SemNet Shiny application.
This procedure generated 1,000 randomized versions of each semantic network to serve as null models for baseline comparisons.
These random networks preserved the number of nodes and edges but removed meaningful semantic organization by randomly rewiring the connections (Christensen & Kenett, 2023).
text.formatted: These random networks preserved the number of nodes and edges but removed meaningful semantic organization by randomly rewiring the connections <ref type="bibr">(Christensen & Kenett, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: We calculated the small-world-ness index (S), which quantifies the extent to which a network simultaneously exhibits high clustering and short ASPL, which are the marks of a small-world structure (Kenett et al., 2016).

Semantic Networks of Politically Extremists versus Politically Moderates
We investigated whether the semantic organization properties related to creativity also underly conspiracy thinking and political extremism.
Our findings partially supported the first hypothesis.
We observed a significant relationship between the tendency to endorse conspiracy theories and political extremism, but contrary to our expectations, this relationship was negative.

In line with our second hypothesis, group-level semantic network comparisons revealed that individuals high in conspiracy thinking exhibited more flexible semantic structure, exemplified by a shorter average shortest path length (ASPL), a higher clustering coefficient (CC), and lower modularity (Q), similar to that found in creative individuals (Kenett et al., 2016).
text.formatted: In line with our second hypothesis, group-level semantic network comparisons revealed that individuals high in conspiracy thinking exhibited more flexible semantic structure, exemplified by a shorter average shortest path length (ASPL), a higher clustering coefficient (CC), and lower modularity (Q), similar to that found in creative individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kenett et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, comparisons of political extremists and political moderates offered partial support for the third hypothesis.
We found some overlap in global network integration between conspiracists and extremists, but not in local associations.
We observed a negative correlation between conspiracy thinking and political extremism.

The surprising direction of this relationship stands in contrast to previous research which suggests a positive association where individuals at both extremes show higher levels of conspiracy endorsement (van Prooijen et al., 2015).
text.formatted: The surprising direction of this relationship stands in contrast to previous research which suggests a positive association where individuals at both extremes show higher levels of conspiracy endorsement <ref type="bibr">(van Prooijen et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: One plausible explanation lies in how political moderates function in the current sociopolitical climate.

Although political moderation is traditionally considered a form of political centrism, it can also reflect forms of political disengagement, distrust or alienation from the political system (Ender & Uscinski, 2021).
text.formatted: Although political moderation is traditionally considered a form of political centrism, it can also reflect forms of political disengagement, distrust or alienation from the political system <ref type="bibr">(Ender & Uscinski, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Research by Abalakina-Paap et al.
(1999) demonstrated that feelings of alienation and institutional distrust are positively related to belief in conspiracies.

Although we did not test for a curvilinear association, in our sample, participants who identified as politically moderate scored higher on the GCBS than those who identified as politically extreme (see Table 2).
text.formatted: Although we did not test for a curvilinear association, in our sample, participants who identified as politically moderate scored higher on the GCBS than those who identified as politically extreme (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: This suggests that the political moderation we observed may not reflect political centrism, but rather disengagement from political ideology.
These individuals may be less trusting of political institutions, parties, and perceived elites, all core traits of conspiracy theorists (Imhoff & Bruder, 2014).
text.formatted: These individuals may be less trusting of political institutions, parties, and perceived elites, all core traits of conspiracy theorists <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Imhoff & Bruder, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In support of this view, some research suggests that many moderate or unaligned voters feel politically "homeless" and are disengaged with both the center-left and center-right, yet also unwilling to endorse far-left or far-right (Harrison, 2020).
text.formatted: In support of this view, some research suggests that many moderate or unaligned voters feel politically "homeless" and are disengaged with both the center-left and center-right, yet also unwilling to endorse far-left or far-right <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Harrison, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Unaffiliated or moderate voters in Europe are less likely to feel represented by mainstream parties, report lower political distrust, and show more disengagement during elections (Bunting, 2024; Hooghe & Kern, 2013; Hooghe et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Unaffiliated or moderate voters in Europe are less likely to feel represented by mainstream parties, report lower political distrust, and show more disengagement during elections <ref type="bibr">(Bunting, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hooghe & Kern, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hooghe et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, individuals who do not feel close to a political party tend to exhibit greater cynicism and alienation (Hooghe & Kern, 2013).
text.formatted: Additionally, individuals who do not feel close to a political party tend to exhibit greater cynicism and alienation <ref type="bibr">(Hooghe & Kern, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This lack of ideological representation may create fertile ground for conspiracy thinking, which is particularly endorsed during times of uncertainty as a way of reestablishing psychological control and coherence (van Prooijen & Krouwel, 2019).
text.formatted: This lack of ideological representation may create fertile ground for conspiracy thinking, which is particularly endorsed during times of uncertainty as a way of reestablishing psychological control and coherence <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(van Prooijen & Krouwel, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Another plausible interpretation of this negative correlation lies in different belief structures characteristic of each construct.
Political extremism is associated with ideologically rigid, internally consistent worldviews (Kruglanski et al., 2006; van Prooijen & Krouwel, 2019).
text.formatted: Political extremism is associated with ideologically rigid, internally consistent worldviews <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kruglanski et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">van Prooijen & Krouwel, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Politically extreme individuals tend to interpret the world through simplified, dichotomous categories and maintain belief systems that are tightly integrated within their ideological agenda (Lammers et al., 2016; van Prooijen & Krouwel, 2019).
text.formatted: Politically extreme individuals tend to interpret the world through simplified, dichotomous categories and maintain belief systems that are tightly integrated within their ideological agenda <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Lammers et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">van Prooijen & Krouwel, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, conspiracy thinking is a monological belief system, wherein belief in one conspiracy increases susceptibility to others, even when they are logically contradictory (Wood et al., 2012).
text.formatted: In contrast, conspiracy thinking is a monological belief system, wherein belief in one conspiracy increases susceptibility to others, even when they are logically contradictory <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Wood et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Conspiracy thinkers appear to prioritize associative pattern recognition over ideological consistency.
For example, some individuals simultaneously believe that Princess Diana was murdered but also that she faked her own death (Wood et al., 2012).
text.formatted: For example, some individuals simultaneously believe that Princess Diana was murdered but also that she faked her own death <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Wood et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This apparent contradiction is ignored to serve the broader narrative of institutional deception (Wood et al., 2012).
text.formatted: This apparent contradiction is ignored to serve the broader narrative of institutional deception <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Wood et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, individuals with high levels of conspiracy thinking in our sample might resist aligning with any fixed political ideology, including extreme ones that offer rigid explanatory frameworks and thus constrain their flexible conspiratorial worldview.
The semantic networks of individuals high in conspiracy belief support the notion of a hyperassociative structure, consistent with our second hypothesis.

Compared to low scorers on the GCBS, high scorers displayed shorter ASPL, lower modularity Q, and greater small-world-ness S. Together, these features indicate a network that is globally integrated and efficiently locally connected.
These features may support lexical access to semantically distant concepts, an organization that is associated with creativity (Kenett et al., 2016).
text.formatted: These features may support lexical access to semantically distant concepts, an organization that is associated with creativity <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kenett et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: We also observed an increase in clustering among high conspiracy believers, which indicates denser local connectivity (Beaty & Kenett, 2023; Benedek et al., 2017; Kenett et al., 2016).
text.formatted: We also observed an increase in clustering among high conspiracy believers, which indicates denser local connectivity <ref type="bibr">(Beaty & Kenett, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Benedek et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kenett et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: While some prior research linked lower clustering to more creative semantic structures, clustering alone in the current context cannot be considered a sign of cognitive rigidity (Kenett et al., 2016).
text.formatted: While some prior research linked lower clustering to more creative semantic structures, clustering alone in the current context cannot be considered a sign of cognitive rigidity <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kenett et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: When interpreted alongside lower modularity, shorter ASPL, and higher small-world-ness, the increased clustering suggests a semantic structure that is both locally associative and globally integrated, which may facilitate associative pattern generation (Beaty & Kenett, 2023; Kenett et al., 2016).
text.formatted: When interpreted alongside lower modularity, shorter ASPL, and higher small-world-ness, the increased clustering suggests a semantic structure that is both locally associative and globally integrated, which may facilitate associative pattern generation <ref type="bibr">(Beaty & Kenett, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kenett et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This interpretation is supported by other studies showing that higher clustering is also indicative of higher small-world-ness and divergent thinking ability (Benedek et al., 201; Rastelli et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This interpretation is supported by other studies showing that higher clustering is also indicative of higher small-world-ness and divergent thinking ability <ref type="bibr">(Benedek et al., 201;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Rastelli et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Theoretical accounts have described conspiracy thinking as a form of associative creativity, in which individuals make uncommon connections (Beaty & Kenett, 2023; Bonetto & Arciszewiski, 2021).
text.formatted: Theoretical accounts have described conspiracy thinking as a form of associative creativity, in which individuals make uncommon connections <ref type="bibr">(Beaty & Kenett, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Bonetto & Arciszewiski, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Empirical studies showed that creative individuals exhibit a small-world network configuration, which facilitates both the clustering and recombination of ideas in novel ways (Kenett et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Empirical studies showed that creative individuals exhibit a small-world network configuration, which facilitates both the clustering and recombination of ideas in novel ways <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kenett et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings suggest that conspiracy thinkers possess semantic organization similar to that of creative individuals.
These findings support a growing body of literature describing conspiracy thinking as an unregulated form of associative processing (Adornetti, 2023; Bonetto & Arciszewski, 2021; Zwaan, 2022).
text.formatted: These findings support a growing body of literature describing conspiracy thinking as an unregulated form of associative processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adornetti, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bonetto & Arciszewski, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Zwaan, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Our analysis of the semantic network structure of political extremists revealed a similar though somewhat different pattern, partially supporting our third hypothesis.
Compared to politically moderate individuals, participants who identified as extreme or strongly committed exhibited shorter ASPL and lower Q, similar to high conspiracy theorists.
Nonetheless, these individuals exhibited no significant differences in clustering.

While we did not conduct a statistical comparison of small-world-ness, the small-world index (S) appears to be nearly identical across the politically extreme and the politically moderate group, suggesting no clear group-level difference in this measure.
Our findings imply that these individuals exhibit a semantic organization that is globally integrated, which supports broad concept retrieval that is not compartmentalized (Kenett et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Our findings imply that these individuals exhibit a semantic organization that is globally integrated, which supports broad concept retrieval that is not compartmentalized <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kenett et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: More importantly, the comparable clustering and small-world-ness indices between politically moderate and extreme individuals suggest that political extremity may not be related to hyper-associative thinking (Benedek et al., 2017).
text.formatted: More importantly, the comparable clustering and small-world-ness indices between politically moderate and extreme individuals suggest that political extremity may not be related to hyper-associative thinking <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Benedek et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The absence of rich local clustering, despite increased global integration, is more consistent with goal-directed, top-down processing than with semantic flexibility (Bar, 2007).
text.formatted: The absence of rich local clustering, despite increased global integration, is more consistent with goal-directed, top-down processing than with semantic flexibility <ref type="bibr">(Bar, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, recent research found that individuals with strong political views show stronger activation in areas linked to response inhibition (Amodoio et al., 2007; Kenett et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Indeed, recent research found that individuals with strong political views show stronger activation in areas linked to response inhibition <ref type="bibr">(Amodoio et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kenett et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This specific aspect lies in contrast to the flexible, locally rich structure we found in conspiracy theorists.
When considered together, the semantic network structures of conspiracy thinkers and political extremists reveal both similarities and differences.
Both groups exhibited shorter ASPL and lower modularity compared to their respective comparison groups.

This finding points to a globally integrated semantic network which suggests that both individuals high in conspiracy thinking and political extremism may possess a heightened capacity for making broad conceptual connections (Benedek et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This finding points to a globally integrated semantic network which suggests that both individuals high in conspiracy thinking and political extremism may possess a heightened capacity for making broad conceptual connections <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Benedek et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This is a property they share with creative individuals (Kenett et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This is a property they share with creative individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kenett et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, only conspiracy thinkers displayed increased local clustering and small-world-ness.
This distinction suggests that individuals with higher levels of conspiracy thinking possess a more flexible and associative semantic network organization.

While the present study is not without methodological limitations, the potential impact of these constraints is mitigated by the theoretical contribution and methodological innovation of our approach.

First, the use of a unidimensional political extremism item did not allow for directional comparisons across the left and the right, which might have obscured ideological asymmetries in associative patterns.
Nonetheless, our focus was on the structural cognitive features of political extremism as a general psychological phenomenon, regardless of political content.
This abstraction is consistent with prior work demonstrating that both ends of the spectrum often share underlying cognitive and motivational traits (van Prooijen & Krouwel, 2019).
text.formatted: This abstraction is consistent with prior work demonstrating that both ends of the spectrum often share underlying cognitive and motivational traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(van Prooijen & Krouwel, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, future research on the semantic organization of political belief systems could benefit from incorporating multi-dimensional ideological measures that allow for comparisons across political content and direction.
This could help clarify whether differences in semantic structure are symmetrical across ideological extremes or whether they vary across ideological commitments.

Similarly, while we collapsed participants into broader categories (strongly committed/extreme versus slightly leaning/moderate) to address sample size limitations, this strategy increased statistical power and preserved interpretability across semantic network metrics.

Importantly, key differences in network properties remained detectable in two distinct analyses: A bootstrapping analysis, showing significant differences in comparisons between generated partial networks, and a random network analysis which confirmed that the patterns we found are meaningful and not random.
This suggests that our findings point to genuine structural distinctions rather than artifacts of classification.
Future research should aim to examine semantic network differences across comparisons between more sharply defined groups.
If the effects observed in this study are reliable, they should be more pronounced in more extreme comparisons.
Another limitation lies in the cross-sectional nature of this study.

We cannot infer the direction of causality in the observed data, and it remains unclear whether the observed semantic organization of conspiracists and extremists serves as a predispositional cognitive feature or whether it is shaped by sustained engagement with such belief systems.
It is also plausible that there is a bidirectional dynamic, in which belief content and semantic organization co-evolve over time.
For example, work by Lodge and Taber (2000) showed that motivated political reasoning influences memory encoding and retrieval.
text.formatted: For example, work by <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Lodge and Taber (2000)</ref> showed that motivated political reasoning influences memory encoding and retrieval.

text.text: Therefore, future research on semantic organization of political and social constructs should consider longitudinal designs to mitigate this directionality issue.
The implications of this research are both theoretically and socially relevant.
This study extends network-based models of cognition into the domain of ideological belief systems.
We demonstrate that semantic network theory can be applied to the study of conspiracy thinking and political extremism.
Theoretically, our findings suggest that these beliefs are not solely driven by social or motivational factors, but they can also manifest at the level of (semantic) cognition.

At a societal level, the findings offer insight into the psychological foundations of increasing polarization and ideological rigidity in contemporary discourse, particularly in political and social contexts.
As partisanship and conspiratorial narratives continue to spread, understanding the underlying cognitive mechanisms which help shape or maintain these beliefs becomes increasingly important.
Our results suggest that targeting the cognitive styles through which these maladaptive beliefs emerge may offer a productive path of intervention.

Since conspiracy thinking appears to be associated with hyper-associative semantic networks, interventions for conspiracists might focus on epistemic discipline and on encouraging these individuals to critically evaluate the connections they draw between concepts.
On the other hand, individuals with extreme political views may respond better to interventions focused on cognitive flexibility that are designed to challenge rigid schemas.
This study offered novel insight at the nexus of conspiracy thinking, political extremism, and semantic organization.

By combining individual differences measures with semantic network analysis, we, to our knowledge, provide the first empirical attempt to explore how semantic cognition relates to political ideology and conspiracy thinking.

Our findings suggest that associative creativity plays a role in conspiracy belief and although political extremists share some of these structural features, their belief systems appear more selectively associative.

Our findings support the growing proposition that conspiracy belief is not a pathological phenomenon but may stem from unregulated cognitive tendencies (Dirzyte, 2023; Huete-Pérez et al., 2025; Zwaan, 2022).
text.formatted: Our findings support the growing proposition that conspiracy belief is not a pathological phenomenon but may stem from unregulated cognitive tendencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Dirzyte, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Huete-Pérez et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Zwaan, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, the present study showed that network science provides a promising framework for understanding the cognitive mechanisms that underlie ideological fragmentation in modern society.
